props.title: Michael
props.initialSlug: Angel with attitude brings romance to small town

sections.content: Michael reimagines angels through John Travolta's earthy, sugar-loving archangel who smells like cookies and loves dancing. Director Nora Ephron crafts a whimsical road movie that stands apart from more serious celestial films like Wings of Desire (1987) or City of Angels (1998). The film taps into a 1990s fascination with angels that included Touched by an Angel (1994-2003) on TV, but takes a distinctly irreverent approach. Travolta's Michael is more interested in women, cigarettes, and bar fights than divine intervention, though his presence still manages to work subtle miracles in the lives of the humans around him.

sections.content: The 1990s saw a surge of angel-themed entertainment that offered varying perspectives on divine intervention. While The Preacher's Wife (1996) gave us Denzel Washington as a dapper, mission-focused angel, and City of Angels (1998) portrayed Nicolas Cage as a love-struck celestial being willing to fall for Meg Ryan, Michael takes the boldest departure. Travolta's angel is deliberately imperfect - he's running out of miracles, his wings are molting, and he can't resist pie. This humanization of the divine became a signature element that influenced later supernatural comedies like Dogma (1999). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Celestial Characters in Cinema

The portrayal of angels in film has ranged from the strictly biblical to the comically human. Constantine (2005) and Legion (2010) present warrior angels in action-horror contexts, while gentler interpretations appear in films like Almost an Angel (1990) with Paul Hogan. Michael bridges these extremes, offering an angel who's powerful enough to slay a bull but spends most of his time dancing to Frank Sinatra. This balance between divine capability and human frailty creates a unique entry in the celestial cinema canon.
